fullText:
Summary: Hayleys PLC (HAYL.N0000) is Sri Lanka's largest diversified group, with businesses from gloves and activated carbon to Singer, shipping and plantations. Profit kept growing in the September 2026 quarter: profit attributable rose 66% to Rs 3.96bn, and for the six months it nearly doubled to Rs 7.53bn (EPS Rs 9.55 against Rs 5.19). At Rs 236.25 the share trades at 1.5x its NAV of Rs 153.11 and 10.2x trailing earnings. But the group's return on equity has averaged only about 11% over ten years (12.4% last year, about 13% annualised this half), and borrowings climbed again to about Rs 334bn as it spent Rs 43.6bn on new plant in six months. With higher profit estimates, the methods now put fair value at about Rs 151 (was Rs 138), so the price is about 56% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 128 and treat under Rs 113 as a strong buy.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 236.25 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-13). Please check it live. Since April 2026 it has traded between Rs 214.00 and Rs 244.00 (Rs 222.00–240.00 in July–September); it was Rs 225.50 at 30 September, against Rs 185.75 a year earlier.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue rose 33% to Rs 358.0bn and profit attributable to shareholders rose 93% to Rs 7.53bn. EPS was Rs 9.55 against Rs 5.19, or Rs 10.07 from continuing operations. The September quarter alone: revenue Rs 178.7bn (up 29%), profit attributable Rs 3.96bn (up 66%), EPS Rs 5.02 against Rs 3.18.
Where the profit came from (segment results, six months): transport and logistics Rs 7.24bn (Rs 3.09bn), consumer and retail (Singer) Rs 8.77bn (Rs 6.13bn), purification (Haycarb) Rs 4.61bn (Rs 2.41bn), gloves Rs 3.25bn (Rs 2.17bn) and industry inputs Rs 0.92bn (Rs 0.51bn). 'Others' was Rs 3.90bn against Rs 4.15bn a year earlier, so June's figure was not a new one-off. Plantations, leisure and tea exports earned less.
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 585.0bn (up 19%), profit attributable Rs 14.05bn, EPS Rs 18.71, return on average equity 12.4%, NAV Rs 150.95, dividends Rs 6.00 (32% of profit). The second half of that year earned Rs 10.15bn, much more than the first, so the year tends to be weighted to October–March.
Debt: borrowings rose to about Rs 334bn at September 2026 (Rs 305bn in June, Rs 290bn in March) against equity of Rs 184bn (including minority interests) and Rs 64bn of cash and deposits. Finance costs rose 89% to Rs 16.2bn in the half year; operating profit covered them about 1.9x. The group spent Rs 43.6bn on property, plant and equipment in six months (Rs 10.4bn a year earlier). Part of the borrowing funds Singer's hire-purchase customers and finance company.
Other: the Maldives hotel sale was completed in June 2026 (Rs 5.4bn received; Rs 0.42bn loss this half). Hayleys Advantis bought three Sri Lankan shipping firms and sold three Maldivian logistics firms, both small. No interim dividend was declared.
History: EPS (after the 2023 10-for-1 split) was Rs 24.34 (2021/22), 21.80, 9.19, 17.91 and 18.71 (2025/26); trailing EPS is now Rs 23.07. ROE averaged about 11% over ten years and about 16% over the last five.

Methods
NAV (Rs 153.11): 1.5x.
Return on equity: 12.4% in 2025/26 and 14.4% in 2024/25; about 13% annualised for April–September 2026.
P/E: 10.2x trailing EPS of Rs 23.07. Year-end P/E: 11.5x (2026), 7.7x (2025).
Dividends: Rs 6.00 a year for the last two years, a 2.5% yield, about a third of profit.
Justified price to book: Rs 61.2 / 114.8 / 191.4, weighted Rs 114.0.
P/E method: Rs 160.0 / 230.0 / 300.0, weighted Rs 223.0.
Residual income: Rs 60.7 / 113.7 / 204.7, weighted Rs 116.0.

Hayleys pays out about a third of its profit, so a dividend model understates it, and its group cash flow is swamped by working capital, capital spending and Singer's lending, so a cash-flow DCF isn't reliable. The book-based methods are much stricter than the P/E method because the group's ROE is below the cost of equity. I haven't done a sum of the parts using the market prices of its listed subsidiaries (Dipped Products, Haycarb, Singer, Alumex and others), which could give a higher figure.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 17.5% / 16% / 15% (a diversified but highly geared group). Unchanged.
Long-run ROE: 10% / 13.5% / 17%. Unchanged.
ROE path (residual income): 13% falling to 10% / 15% falling to 13.5% / 17% staying at 17%. Raised from 12% / 14% / 16% for the first year, because the half-year results point to about 15% this year in the base case.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%. Unchanged.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 20 × 8 / 23 × 10 / 25 × 12. Raised from 17 / 20 / 23: Rs 9.55 is already earned, and the second half has been the stronger one (Rs 13.52 last year, or about Rs 12.75 on today's larger share count).
Average of the three methods: Rs 94.0 / Rs 152.8 / Rs 232.0.
Common: Sri Lankan government bonds yield about 11% (the interim report quotes 10.91–11.20% for comparable government securities at September 2026). Payout 32%. Per-share figures use 795mn shares.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 151 (1.0x NAV), up from Rs 138, so Rs 236.25 is about 56% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 128.35, and 25% gives Rs 113.25.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 151.00, 150 at up to Rs 128.35 and 150 at up to Rs 113.25. That averages about Rs 132.88, about Rs 66,440, against Rs 118,125 at Rs 236.25.
Realism: Rs 151 needs about a 36% fall. Since April 2026 the share has traded between Rs 214 and Rs 244, so it is not likely soon; it would take a market fall or a profit setback.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 15%: 63.7 / 121.9 / 201.5 for long-run ROE of 10% / 13.5% / 17%.
Cost of equity 16%: 56.8 / 106.7 / 174.6.
Cost of equity 17.5%: 48.7 / 89.3 / 143.9.
Today's price needs ROE of about 19–20% for many years at a 16% cost of equity.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: ROE staying above 15% for a full year (the last 12 months come close, helped by the strong second half of last year); borrowings falling once the new plant is paid for; lower interest rates, which help a group this geared; selling weaker businesses, as with the Maldives hotel; a sum of the parts showing listed subsidiaries worth well above book.
Supports a lower value: a global slowdown hitting gloves, carbon and textiles exports; a stronger rupee cutting export profits; rising interest rates, with finance costs already up 89%; bad debts at Singer; more one-off losses, or the jump in logistics profit fading.

Business tests: 1 of 4 passed (unchanged), so it stays in "avoid for now". Return on equity fails (12.4% last full year, about 11% over ten years); debt fails (net debt 1.5x equity); steady profit passes; cash fails (operating cash flow Rs 7.3bn against profit of Rs 13.2bn in the half year, after a negative year).

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
